text: There is a famous result called the universal approximation theorem. It says that a network with a single hidden layer, given enough neurons, can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region as closely as you like. If one wide layer is already enough in principle, why does every modern network, including every language model, stack dozens of layers instead?

The catch is hidden in the words enough neurons. A single hidden layer builds its function by adding up hinges side by side, and each ReLU neuron contributes at most one new corner. For a function with many wiggles, the width you need can grow enormously, because a shallow network has no way to reuse a piece of work it has already done; every wiggle has to be paid for separately.

Depth gives the network a way to reuse work, and the clearest picture of it is folding. Take a tent-shaped function on the interval from zero to one. It rises to the top in the middle and comes back down, so it folds the interval in half, sending both halves onto the whole interval. A tent like this can be built from just two ReLU neurons.

Now apply the tent a second time, to its own output. Every point of the interval has already been folded once, so folding again doubles the number of teeth, and a third application doubles them again. Like folding a sheet of paper, each new fold takes almost no extra effort yet doubles the number of creases, so with only two neurons per layer, the number of straight pieces grows exponentially with the number of layers.

Compare that with a single wide layer working on one input. With n ReLU neurons it can make at most n plus one straight pieces, because each neuron adds one corner, so matching ten layers of folding would take about a thousand neurons side by side. This gap is not a curiosity: theorists have proved that some functions computed by deep, narrow networks need exponentially many neurons when the network is shallow.

Real data seems to reward this kind of reuse. In image networks, early layers detect edges, middle layers combine edges into textures and parts, and later layers combine parts into objects, so each concept is built once and reused by everything above it. Depth has a price, though, because signals must travel through every layer during training, and the next few lessons are about keeping those signals healthy.

A language model works the same way, as a deep stack of blocks, each one refining every token's vector a little further. So depth helps because each layer can build on what the layers before it have computed, folding the space again instead of starting from scratch. Next we write the forward pass of a network as a computational graph, the structure that makes training possible.
